title: THE ECO OFFICE: Dynamic and Homeostatic Façades inspired by BIOMORPHISM, BIOMIMICRY, AND BIOPHILIA
central_proposition: This dissertation proposes that integrating nature-inspired design principles (Biomorphism, Biomimicry, Biophilia) and nanotechnology into building facades can create responsive, dynamic, and homeostatic environments that enhance human comfort and evoke positive psychophysiological responses, particularly in tropical settings.

concept_definitions.name: Biomimicry
concept_definitions.definition: A new science studying nature by imitating or taking inspiration from existing design models and processes to solve human problems; innovation inspired by nature.

concept_definitions.name: Biophilia
concept_definitions.definition: An innate affiliation with nature, or 'love of nature, of living organisms', rooted in an inborn predisposition for certain natural stimuli.

concept_definitions.name: Psychophysiology
concept_definitions.definition: The study of mind-body interactions, using physiological measures to understand human responses to environmental stimuli.

concept_definitions.name: Nanotechnology
concept_definitions.definition: A field that explores material and system science at molecular levels, leading to new methods, systems, and properties previously undiscovered, involving research and technology development at the 1nm-100nm ranges.

concept_definitions.name: Biomorphism
concept_definitions.definition: The application of nature inspiration, specifically the 'design spiral' and 'leaf' within plant/tree systems, to building design modules, focusing on form and morphology.

concept_definitions.name: Adaptive Comfort
concept_definitions.definition: The concept that the comfort zone for indoor temperatures shifts with outdoor weather, particularly in environments where occupants have adaptive opportunities (e.g., operable windows).

argument_structure: The argument is structured in three parts: Biomorphism (nature-inspired forms and morphology), Biomimicry (materials and performance through nanotechnology and simulations), and Biophilia (human psychophysiological and psychological responses). It progresses from conceptual inspiration, to material and system implementation and performance analysis, and finally to human validation of the designs.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core causal logic is that by emulating nature's forms, processes, and ecosystems (Biomimicry) at both macro and nano scales (Biomorphism), building facades can become dynamic and responsive. This responsiveness allows for passive regulation of light, air, and heat, leading to homeostatic interior conditions. These nature-inspired, comfortable environments, in turn, leverage humans' innate biophilic tendencies, eliciting positive psychophysiological responses (e.g., calmness, attention, pleasure) and contributing to overall wellbeing and sustainability.

findings.antecedent: Biomimicry (nature-inspired concepts) at macro and micro/nano molecular scales
findings.consequent: Maximized thermal comfort, creation of responsive, dynamic building envelopes
findings.mechanism: Inspiration from natural systems and organisms provides design models and processes for efficient material and system solutions. Nanotechnology enables control at molecular levels for novel material properties, contributing to environmental regulation.
findings.source: 1.1 Introduction, p. 16
findings.quote: How can we employ biomimicry (nature-inspired concepts) at the macro and micro/nano molecular scales (latter with nanotechnologies), in order to maximize THERMAL COMFORT, and create a more RESPONSIVE, DYNAMIC building envelope in the tropics?
findings.empirical_support_cited: The dissertation tests this through design simulations and psychophysiological experiments.

findings.antecedent: Sites and buildings designed incorporating Biomorphic, Biomimetic, and Biophilic strategies
findings.consequent: More effective, responsive, dynamic built environments
findings.mechanism: These integrated strategies enable buildings to function like living organisms, adapting to climate and topography, regulating temperature and humidity, and evoking positive human responses due to an innate connection to nature.
findings.source: 1.2 Goals and Objectives, p. 16
findings.quote: The work of this dissertation will test the hypothesis that sites and buildings, designed incorporating: Biomorphic, Biomimetic, and Biophilic strategies, will serve to function more effectively as relevant examples of a responsive, dynamic built environment...
findings.empirical_support_cited: The dissertation tests this hypothesis through design prototypes and experimental analysis.

findings.antecedent: Specific nature-based architectural cues
findings.consequent: Responsive concepts in architectural sustainability
findings.mechanism: Delineating and designing these elements through interactive concepts and effective incorporation leads to healthier and more sustainable architectural solutions.
findings.source: 1.5 Dissertation Hypotheses, p. 27
findings.quote: The hypothesis of this research is that there are some specific nature-based architectural cues that can be incorporated in building technologies.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The research aims to delineate these elements and test their impact.

findings.antecedent: Nanotechnology
findings.consequent: Environmentally-responsive building facades (thermal comfort, natural daylighting, passive ventilation)
findings.mechanism: Nanomaterials and systems offer novel properties at molecular levels, allowing for advanced regulation of light, air, and heat transfer in building envelopes, addressing issues like thermal comfort and passive ventilation.
findings.source: 1.4.4 Biomimicry: Nanotechnology and Architectural Design, p. 24
findings.quote: The idea behind implementing green design technologies for a tropical setting is to address the issue of thermal comfort, natural daylighting, and passive ventilation, to implement environmentally-responsive building façades and envelopes.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Literature review on nanotechnology applications in architecture (e.g., nanospiked surfaces, microcapsules, nano vent-skin).

findings.antecedent: Nature-inspired design
findings.consequent: Positive emotional responses (calmness, focus, attention, low stress, happiness)
findings.mechanism: Humans have an innate predisposition (biophilia) to affiliate with nature, and nature-based environments provide restorative potential, reducing physiological and psychological stress and promoting positive affective states.
findings.source: 1.4.5 Biophilia: Psychophysiology and Architectural Design, p. 25
findings.quote: The objective behind the researcher's attention to the “ECO” aspect is to investigate and create a digital design prototype that would enable designers to create enriching spaces that will not merely prove functional, but also evoke and arouse positive emotional responses in humans.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Psychophysiological experiments (EEG, ECG, EMG, GSR) are used to assess these responses.

findings.antecedent: Certain spatial configurations and patterns within the built environment
findings.consequent: More positive emotional responses in users
findings.mechanism: These configurations align with human innate preferences for natural elements, contributing to feelings of comfort and aesthetic appeal, as described by cognitive processes like Coherence, Complexity, Legibility, and Mystery.
findings.source: 1.4.5 Biophilia: Psychophysiology and Architectural Design, p. 25
findings.quote: The ontological basis for this research is that there are some specific nature-based architectural cues that can be incorporated in building technologies, and that certain spatial configurations and patterns within the built environment do evoke more positive emotional responses in users of such spaces or areas than others...
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies based on Kaplans' research defined spatial configurations in terms of cognitive processes.

findings.antecedent: Natural elements (savannas, water-features, vegetation, flowers)
findings.consequent: Awareness, positive emotional states
findings.mechanism: Humans have an inborn predisposition to like such natural elements, as appropriate emotional responses to these features contributed to survival in evolutionary history.
findings.source: 2.2.2 Morphology, Geometry, and Nature-Inspired Designs, p. 50
findings.quote: Humans seem to display a consistent preference for four types of natural contents: savannas, water-features, vegetation, and flowers. Importantly, the widespread aesthetic appeal of these elements is found to be suggestive of an inborn predisposition to like such natural elements.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Literature on landscape aesthetics and human preference for natural contents.

findings.antecedent: Presence of landscape features and plants in interior spaces (e.g., offices)
findings.consequent: Increased aesthetic appeal, increased feeling of comfort
findings.mechanism: These features align with human innate preferences for natural elements, contributing to positive emotional states and a sense of wellbeing in the built environment.
findings.source: 2.2.2 Morphology, Geometry, and Nature-Inspired Designs, p. 50
findings.quote: For example, in interior spaces, such as offices, the presence of landscape features and plants is found to increase the aesthetic appeal and feeling of comfort of the setting.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited studies found that the presence of landscape features and plants increases aesthetic appeal and comfort in interior spaces.

findings.antecedent: Vegetated urban landscapes (especially with trees or a water feature)
findings.consequent: Higher preference compared to non-vegetated (human-made, urban) architectural settings
findings.mechanism: The presence of natural elements aligns with human innate preferences and restorative needs, which are often lacking in modern, non-vegetated urban environments.
findings.source: 2.2.2 Morphology, Geometry, and Nature-Inspired Designs, p. 50
findings.quote: Among vegetated landscapes and environments in urban settings, it was also found that those urban settings that also contain some vegetation (especially trees) or a water feature are preferred most.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies found that vegetated urban settings are preferred, contrasting with modern built environments that lack natural geometry.

findings.antecedent: Merely mimicking natural form (superficial application of characteristics)
findings.consequent: Misses the idea of biomimetic design, disregards the wholeness of natural form
findings.mechanism: True biomimicry requires a holistic understanding of nature's form, underlying processes, and ecosystem interactions, not just superficial imitation, to achieve seamless engagement with the natural world.
findings.source: 2.2.3 The Bio-Inspiration “Spark”: Leaf Morphology, p. 54
findings.quote: Benyus writes that “a full emulation of nature engages at least three levels of mimicry: form, process, and ecosystem”.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Benyus (1997) warns that 'a full emulation of nature engages at least three levels of mimicry: form, process, and ecosystem'.

findings.antecedent: Leaf morphology (e.g., sun/shade leaf arrangements, top/bottom leaf arrangements)
findings.consequent: Strategies for light and heat regulation in building design
findings.mechanism: Leaves adapt their shape, thickness, and porosity to optimize light absorption (e.g., notched outer leaves for light penetration, broader shade leaves for diffuse radiation) and dissipate heat (e.g., smaller, lobed sun leaves for convection), maintaining internal temperature stability. These adaptations can inspire building facade designs.
findings.source: 2.2.3 The Bio-Inspiration “Spark”: Leaf Morphology, p. 55-56
findings.quote: Studies on leaf placement, position, and hierarchy within the tree’s longitudinal cross-section and latitudinal structure (cross canopy) revealed some interesting trends in leaf evolution...
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies on leaf placement, position, hierarchy, and evolution reveal trends in light and heat adaptation.

findings.antecedent: Heliotropism in plants (tracking sun's movements)
findings.consequent: More efficient, passive solar panels
findings.mechanism: Mimicking plants' ability to track the sun's movement allows solar panels to optimize their angle for maximum solar radiation absorption without external power, using materials that change properties in response to temperature fluctuations.
findings.source: 2.3.3 Biomimetics and Nanotech: Applications in Design, p. 71-72
findings.quote: Biomimicry of heliotropic plants – more efficient solar panels. Current solar-tracking-photovoltaic panels include the utilization of engines and electronic control frameworks, yet a biomimetic heliotropic photovoltaic panel can now be made with the utilization of several alternativc materials and designs, ones that are much more affordable.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Student team 'Heliotrope' from MIT designed an inexpensive, passive solar-tracking device.

findings.antecedent: Photoperiodism in plants (responding to day/night length)
findings.consequent: Light-activated actuators for building facades
findings.mechanism: Plants use pigmented proteins (phytochromes) to sense day length and change shape; this can be translated into materials (e.g., graphene nanoplatelets) that reversibly expand/contract in response to light, regulating light levels in building facades.
findings.source: 2.3.3 Biomimetics and Nanotech: Applications in Design, p. 74-75
findings.quote: Graphene’s incredible discovery in 2004 led to intense analysis and scrutiny of its superior mechanical, structural, and thermal properties. Various scientists have been working on photomechanical actuators that are infused or integrated with graphene nanoplatelets that would then respond to achieve strains or tactile pressures upon illumination.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Researchers developed graphene nanoplatelet-based photomechanical actuators that respond to near-infrared illumination.

findings.antecedent: Stomatal transpiration (leaf pores regulating air movement)
findings.consequent: 'Breathable' building envelopes for natural ventilation and moisture control
findings.mechanism: Guard cells in stomata regulate pore opening to control air and moisture exchange; this can be mimicked in facade openings or materials (e.g., 'Stomatex' fabric) to regulate indoor air quality and humidity.
findings.source: 2.3.3 Biomimetics and Nanotech: Applications in Design, p. 78
findings.quote: Instead of windows, building envelopes might be better served equipped with “stomata-like” openings on the facades, for instance, the “Stomatex” fabric.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The concept of 'Stomatex' fabric is cited as an example.

findings.antecedent: Thigmonastic movement in plants (responding to touch)
findings.consequent: Kinetic building envelopes that respond to tactile stimuli (e.g., water/wind)
findings.mechanism: Plants use turgor pressure changes in specialized cells to move in response to touch; this can be translated into 'ultra-sensitive' sensors (e.g., synthetic cricket hairs, PVDF microbelts) and actuators for dynamic facade elements that respond to environmental cues.
findings.source: 2.3.3 Biomimetics and Nanotech: Applications in Design, p. 81-83
findings.quote: It may be possible to employ moisture-control valves located on external building facades to regulate moisture inside spaces. If possible, “ultra-sensitive” tracking sensors on the façade of the building could control these valves, so that the system updates continually as it responds to external changes and influences within the environment.
findings.empirical_support_cited: University researchers at Wisconsin-Madison established a small mechanism to convert human breath airflow into electricity, and synthetic cricket hairs were developed as ultra-sensitive airflow sensors.

findings.antecedent: Shape variation in leaves for thermoregulation (e.g., smaller, thicker, lobed sun leaves)
findings.consequent: Façade changes for heat dissipation
findings.mechanism: Sun leaves adapt to dissipate heat by being smaller, thicker, and more deeply lobed, creating thinner boundary layers of heated air; this can inform facade design to regulate heat transfer convectively.
findings.source: 2.3.3 Biomimetics and Nanotech: Applications in Design, p. 85
findings.quote: Sun leaves on some trees have adapted to dissipate more heat by being smaller, thicker, and more deeply lobed. This makes the surface of a sun leaf a shorter distance from a free edge; and, since the boundary layer thickness increases with distance from an edge, it will have a thinner boundary layer of heated air.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies show that varying leaf shape characteristics makes sun leaves significantly better heat exchangers.

findings.antecedent: Color change in amphibians for thermoregulation
findings.consequent: Building skins that change color/opacity for light/heat regulation
findings.mechanism: Amphibians use iridophore cells to alter reflectivity for thermoregulation; this can be mimicked in dichromatic/polychromatic building skins to adjust light transmittance and radiant heating within interiors.
findings.source: 2.3.3 Biomimetics and Nanotech: Applications in Design, p. 87
findings.quote: The African reed frog, as with many other amphibians, also uses iridophore cells for reflectance. This is because the arrangement of iridophore cells in layers that run parallel to the skin surface maximizes reflectivity of solar radiation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: African reed frog and green tree frog use iridophore cells for reflectance and rapid thermally induced color change.

findings.antecedent: Porous nanocoatings (e.g., Vanadium dioxide (VO2) films)
findings.consequent: Smart windows that transition from transparent to metallic states for solar modulation
findings.mechanism: VO2 exhibits thermochromic properties, transitioning from transparent (low temp) to metallic (high temp) while allowing visible light, effectively regulating infrared radiation. Altering nano-level properties like porosity enhances performance.
findings.source: 2.3.3 Biomimetics and Nanotech: Applications in Design, p. 87-88
findings.quote: Vanadium dioxide (VO2) has, as a relatively new material, has generated substantial technological relevance for the fields of optics and electronics, and as a favorable contender for producing smart windows...
findings.empirical_support_cited: Research shows VO2 films can transition phase at ~68 degrees Celsius, with enhanced luminous transmittance and solar modulating ability.

findings.antecedent: Natural settings (vs. urban scenes)
findings.consequent: Higher alpha amplitudes (EEG), lower heart rates (ECG)
findings.mechanism: Nature provides restorative experiences that reduce physiological arousal and promote wakeful relaxation and focused attention, as indicated by brain wave activity and heart rate changes.
findings.source: 2.4.3 Psychophysiology and Human Responses, p. 98
findings.quote: Specifically, alpha amplitudes were higher when subjects viewed slides with vegetation rather than urban scenes. This is significant since alpha waves are a valid indicator of brain activation and is associated with wakeful relaxation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies show higher alpha amplitudes and a trend for higher heart rate activity when subjects viewed slides with vegetation rather than urban scenes.

findings.antecedent: Nature scenes
findings.consequent: Inspired arousal, thoughtful, contemplative consideration
findings.mechanism: Nature's complexity and legibility (Kaplan's model) provide opportunities for both understanding and exploration, engaging cognitive processes and fostering a sense of mystery.
findings.source: 2.4.3 Psychophysiology and Human Responses, p. 100
findings.quote: Ulrich accepts that the aforementioned discoveries are concurrent with view that nature scenes are more fruitful in inspiring arousal and thoughtful, contemplative consideration.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Ulrich accepts that nature scenes are more fruitful in inspiring arousal and thoughtful, contemplative consideration.

findings.antecedent: Nature-based environments
findings.consequent: Reduced stress, restored directed attention
findings.mechanism: Nature provides 'soft fascination' and a sense of 'being away,' allowing directed attention fatigue to recover and promoting psychological restoration.
findings.source: 2.4.3 Psychophysiology and Human Responses, p. 101-102
findings.quote: Investigations demonstrated that the avoidance tape was fruitful in inspiring both mental and physiological anxiety. Estimation of three physiological variables (PTT, SCR and EMG) throughout the recuperation stage uncovered a speedier and more complete anxiety recuperation when subjects were faced with nature-based, rather than urban sceneries.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Ulrich et al. studies on stressed individuals showed speedier and more complete anxiety recuperation in nature-based sceneries.

findings.antecedent: Presence of vegetative components (plants)
findings.consequent: Improved cognitive working (quicker response times)
findings.mechanism: Vegetative elements positively impact attention and focus, leading to better task performance and cognitive function.
findings.source: 2.4.3 Psychophysiology and Human Responses, p. 102
findings.quote: Lohr et al. uncovered through studies that subjects felt more thoughtful and attentive when they had performed a test in a room with plants, contrasted with subjects that made the test where plants were absent or removed.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Lohr et al. studies showed subjects felt more thoughtful and attentive and had quicker response times in rooms with plants.

findings.antecedent: High levels of vegetation/greenery in public housing
findings.consequent: Reduced total crimes, property crimes, violent crimes
findings.mechanism: Nature provides restorative effects, potentially reducing aggression, increasing social cohesion, or improving surveillance, thereby positively impacting community safety.
findings.source: 2.4.3 Psychophysiology and Human Responses, p. 103
findings.quote: Buildings with high levels of vegetation had 52% fewer total crimes, 48% fewer property crimes, and 56% fewer violent crimes than buildings with low levels of vegetation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: A study by Kuo and Sullivan correlated greenery levels with crime rates in public housing.

findings.antecedent: Curved lines and forms (in built environment)
findings.consequent: 'Affiliative' aspects, higher information content, evoked comfort
findings.mechanism: Curved forms reflect an inborn predilection for natural-like forms and patterns, which are perceived as less hostile and moderately complex, leading to positive emotional valences and a sense of comfort.
findings.source: 2.4.4 Biophilic Design, p. 107
findings.quote: It was discovered that straight forms were prevalently connected with hostile attributes, while curved lines and forms were correlated with "affiliative" aspects. ... A decidedly agreeable theory by Salingaros states that curves are higher in information content, and thereby respond to our need for moderately complex information.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies indicate straight forms are linked to hostile attributes, while curved forms are linked to 'affiliative' aspects. Salingaros states curves have higher information content.

findings.antecedent: Hybrid Module (AB) design (combination of angle and porosity dynamism)
findings.consequent: Ideal adaptation to light, wind, heat; achievement of homeostasis and equilibrium within interior spaces
findings.mechanism: Dynamic responsiveness through alterations in both angle and porosity allows the module to adapt effectively to changing environmental conditions (solar path, wind patterns), regulating interior daylighting, ventilation, and thermal comfort.
findings.source: 4.5.4 Dissertation Research Summary and Final Points, p. 190
findings.quote: Performance levels of this module, when compared against the other two façade modules (A and B), proved that dynamic responsiveness utilization of alterations in both angle and porosity as adaptive techniques was the ideal method of achieving homeostasis and conditions of equilibrium within the interior spaces of the “Eco-Office”.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Simulation analysis (daylighting, CFD, thermal) showed the Hybrid Module excelled in performance.

findings.antecedent: Hybrid (AB) and Rectangular (A) modules
findings.consequent: Higher EMG (Smile) response (more pleasurable)
findings.mechanism: The dynamic and responsive nature of these modules, potentially offering a sense of control or engaging visual interest without overload, aligns with human preferences for dynamism and visual comfort, leading to positive affective measures.
findings.source: 4.4 Biophilia: Analysis and Discussion, p. 196
findings.quote: The greater the EMG activity, the larger is action potential among the respondents, which displays evidence of the fact that the respondents viewed the Hybrid and Rectangular modules to be more pleasurable than the Base and Organic modules.
findings.empirical_support_cited: EMG (Smile) results showed Hybrid (AB) > Rectangular (A) > Organic (B) > Base (O).

findings.antecedent: Hybrid (AB) and Rectangular (A) modules
findings.consequent: Higher alpha brain activity (wakeful relaxation)
findings.mechanism: The dynamic forms of these modules, by providing engaging visual stimuli without causing cognitive overload, promote a state of wakeful relaxation, as indicated by increased alpha activity in the brain.
findings.source: 4.4 Biophilia: Analysis and Discussion, p. 193-195
findings.quote: The greater the alpha activity, the larger was the indication of calmness and “wakeful relaxation” among the respondents, further indicating evidence of the fact that the respondents viewed the dynamic forms (Hybrid module, Rectangular module) to be more relaxing than the static forms (Organic module, Base module).
findings.empirical_support_cited: EEG (Left) and EEG (Right) results showed significant differences, with Hybrid and Rectangular modules indicating greater calmness and wakeful relaxation.

findings.antecedent: Organic Module (B) imagery
findings.consequent: Decreased heart rates (calming, attention-focusing effects)
findings.mechanism: The organic, porous, and 'screen-like' nature of the module, reminiscent of natural functions and offering appreciated lighting quality, may evoke a sense of calm and positively engage viewer attention.
findings.source: 4.4 Biophilia: Analysis and Discussion, p. 192
findings.quote: Both sets of Organic Module imagery (B1, B2, B3) and Hybrid Module imagery (AB1, AB2, AB3) caused a corresponding decrease in heart rates, compared to baseline activity of the respondents. This decrease was stronger for the Organic Module images, indicating that the stimuli presented were quite calming and also tended to focus the viewer’s attention.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Heart rate analysis showed a decrease in heart rates for Organic Module images, indicating calming and attention-focusing effects.

findings.antecedent: Base Module (O) imagery
findings.consequent: Strongest increase in heart rates (high arousal, stimulus rejection)
findings.mechanism: The 'stark nature' and unfamiliarity of the base design, lacking nature-inspired qualities, may trigger a defensive response or heightened physiological arousal in viewers.
findings.source: 4.4 Biophilia: Analysis and Discussion, p. 192
findings.quote: BASE Module (O1 exterior view, O2 elevation) imagery elicited the strongest increase in value changes (degree of activation and orientation) compared to baseline activity/data (see Tables XIV, XV). This indicates that these images were highly arousing and prone to stimulus rejection, probably due to the unfamiliarity of the design images, or due to the stark nature of the images.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Heart rate analysis showed Base Module imagery elicited the strongest increase in value changes compared to baseline activity.

findings.antecedent: Design images with 'Nature' component, 'Dynamism,' and 'Comfort' levels
findings.consequent: Higher preference ranking than pure aesthetics
findings.mechanism: Human preference is driven by deeper, innate connections to nature (Biophilia) and functional benefits (dynamism, comfort) that contribute to wellbeing, rather than superficial aesthetic qualities alone.
findings.source: 4.5.4 Dissertation Research Summary and Final Points, p. 191
findings.quote: The “Nature” component and “Dymamism” and “Comfort” levels were found to be ranked higher than pure aesthetics with design images that evoked experiences and relationship with nature.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Overall responses indicated 'Nature' component, 'Dynamism,' and 'Comfort' levels were ranked higher than pure aesthetics.

findings.antecedent: Nature-based environments (Biomorphism, Biomimicry, Biophilia)
findings.consequent: Superior sustainable design processes
findings.mechanism: An integrated approach drawing from nature's principles leads to designs that achieve dynamism, homeostasis, and a deeper connection to nature, surpassing conventional methods focused merely on reducing negative impacts.
findings.source: 4.5.4 Dissertation Research Summary and Final Points, p. 191
findings.quote: Furthermore, the Biomimicry and Biophilia components strongly attested to the overall premise of this dissertation: that nature and nature-based environments are superior to conventional design processes in a variety of ways so that a sustainable design created out of a combination of Biomorphism, Biomimicry, and Biophilia does indeed accomplish the following goals...
findings.empirical_support_cited: The dissertation's synthesis of findings supports this claim.

findings.antecedent: Integrating naturalness in modern habitats (through realistic representations of nature)
findings.consequent: Enhanced wellbeing, pleasure, restorative power for humans
findings.mechanism: Modern urban environments often lack natural characteristics, depriving humans of a source of wellbeing and restorative power; realistic representations of nature can evoke biophilic reactions, restoring psychological, physiological, and cognitive functioning.
findings.source: 4.5.4 Dissertation Research Summary and Final Points, p. 188
findings.quote: Therefore, if it is not possible to integrate real natural contents in a setting, then it could be valuable to implement realistic representations of nature. This discussion underscores the importance of integrating naturalness in our current modern habitats.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Empirical research indicates that almost exact simulations of nature, and even artistic interpretations of natural settings, are capable of inducing biophilic reactions.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Sites and buildings designed incorporating Biomorphic, Biomimetic, and Biophilic strategies will function more effectively as responsive, dynamic built environments.
Specific nature-based architectural cues can be delineated and incorporated into building technologies to create responsive concepts in architectural sustainability.
The proposed design will achieve dynamism, contribute to homeostasis, and effectively 'reach back to nature'.
The design prototype will demonstrate energy efficiency in daylighting, natural ventilation, and thermal comfort for a tropical site in Honolulu.
People's preferences and psychophysiological responses to the architectural urban prototype in Honolulu can be determined and correlated with specific design elements, characteristics, and patterns.
bridge_warrants: The dissertation explicitly connects Biomorphism (form), Biomimicry (materials and processes), and Biophilia (human response) as an integrated triad for sustainable design.
It bridges psychophysiology with architectural design by using physiological measures to validate the human affective responses to nature-inspired building facades.
It links nanotechnology advancements to biomimetic principles for novel material applications in building envelopes.
methodological_critiques: Previous psychophysiology studies often used primitive controls and measures, leading to longer study periods and habituation effects.

The dissertation acknowledges 'grey areas or unidentified entities within the analysis of “looping”', specifically regarding how building facade designs might affect and effect changes and adaptations in the external environment (internal to external feedback loop).
model_structure: The dissertation proposes a 'Challenge to Biology' Design Spiral (CBS) as a series of checkpoints for the biomimetic design process (Identify, Interpret, Discover, Abstract, Emulate, Evaluate, Identify). It also conceptualizes a 'triad system' of Biomorphism, Biomimicry, and Biophilia as interconnected components for achieving sustainable design.
limitations: Visual simulations may not accurately replicate or reflect the final performance of the building.
The analysis of 'looping' (internal to external environmental effects) still contains 'grey areas' or unidentified entities.
The research acknowledges a fair amount of speculation and hypothetical theorizing regarding the three topics.
